passage:
Interviewer: What got you through that quarter?

Honestly, Ishita. I'm Aditi, and last winter the company was running out of money, and I stopped sleeping. I sent Ishita a message at midnight saying, "I don't know what to do." She didn't tell me it would be fine. She said, "I can't promise a rescue. But I'll sit with you while you look at the numbers." And she did, every Thursday for three months.

She told me some hard things. That I was avoiding a difficult conversation with my co-founder. That I hired too fast. I didn't like hearing it, but I wrote it all down.

I thanked her at the time, but I also wrote to her afterwards with what I changed. I cut two costs, I had the conversation with my co-founder. Thanks matter more when they turn into action.

qa.q: How often did Ishita meet Aditi during the dark quarter?
qa.a: Ishita met Aditi every Thursday for three months.

qa.q: Why did Aditi message Ishita at midnight, and what was Aditi feeling?
qa.a: Aditi was overwhelmed and not sleeping because the company was running out of money, and wrote 'I don't know what to do.'

qa.q: What did Aditi do to show gratitude that lasts?
qa.a: Aditi listened to the hard truths, changed things such as costs and the co-founder conversation, and reported back to Ishita with the outcomes.

qa.q: How might Ishita have felt about telling Aditi hard truths?
qa.a: Ishita may have felt it was risky to say them, but offering honesty without a promise of rescue shows care more than easy comfort would.

grounding: A mentor stays through a dark quarter without promising rescue; Aditi thanks her specifically, listens to hard truths and reports back on outcomes.

passage:
Bhupen's diary, 14 Dec.
Worst quarter yet. Two clients gone, payroll barely met.
Sonali-ma'am called anyway. She's been my mentor since the college accelerator. She never once said "it'll be fine". Today she said, "Your pricing is too low and you know it. You're scared to raise it." That hurt. Also true.
She stayed on the call an hour. Didn't offer money. Didn't offer to fix anything. Just asked hard questions until I had my own answers.
Things I'm doing because of her:
- raising the price for new clients from January
- dropping the custom-app work that eats all our time
- sending her an update on the 31st, whatever happens
Also, I finally wrote her a proper thank-you. Not "thanks for everything". I wrote: "Thank you for telling me the pricing truth when I didn't want to hear it. That call changed our December."
Grateful. Still scared.

qa.q: What did Sonali-ma'am say about Bhupen's pricing?
qa.a: "Your pricing is too low and you know it. You're scared to raise it."

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling after the call?
qa.a: Bhupen felt grateful and still scared, stung by the hard truth but thankful for it.

qa.q: How is Bhupen showing gratitude beyond just praise?
qa.a: By acting on the advice, writing a specific thank-you, and promising to update Sonali-ma'am on the 31st.

qa.q: How might Sonali-ma'am feel reading Bhupen's thank-you?
qa.a: She may feel touched and respected, knowing her hard truths were heard and put to use.

grounding: A mentor stays through a dark quarter without promising rescue; the protagonist thanks her specifically, listens to hard truths and plans to update her.
